nodes.name: Sunlight
nodes.desc: Powers the algae of the sunlit sea and the dense forest canopy of the island.

nodes.name: Heavy rainfall
nodes.desc: Over 7,000 mm of rain a year feeds more than 200 waterfalls and the cloud forest, the only humid tropical forest on an oceanic island in the region.

nodes.name: Ocean currents
nodes.desc: The island is the first landmark met by the North Equatorial Countercurrent, where currents meet and carry larvae and plankton across the Pacific.

nodes.name: Decomposers
nodes.desc: Fungi, bacteria and insects break down dead leaves, wood and carcasses, returning nutrients to the thin acidic island soil.

nodes.name: Phytoplankton
nodes.desc: Microscopic algae in the sunlit water around the island, the base of the open-ocean food chain.

nodes.name: Miconia shrubs
nodes.desc: A genus of berry-bearing shrubs and small trees. Miconia are among the most recorded plants in the cloud forest, which is dominated by Melastomataceae.

nodes.name: Coconut palm
nodes.desc: Coastal forest is dominated partly by coconut palm, along with purple coral tree and pond apple.

nodes.name: Copepods
nodes.desc: Tiny crustaceans that graze phytoplankton in the plankton-rich waters of the island, food for fish and whale sharks.

nodes.name: Flying fish
nodes.desc: Plankton-feeding fish that leap from the water to escape predators. A staple prey of boobies, frigatebirds and tuna.

nodes.name: Cocos finch
nodes.desc: Found only on Cocos Island, it eats berries and insects and uses varied foraging methods learned from other finches.

nodes.name: White-tailed deer
nodes.desc: Introduced by people; the island has no native land mammals. Deer browse native plants and are a management concern.

nodes.name: Wild boar
nodes.desc: Introduced pigs root through the forest and damage native plants and animals; control efforts continue.

nodes.name: Black rat
nodes.desc: An introduced omnivore on the island, listed among the invasive species that harm native wildlife.

nodes.name: Ambrosia beetles
nodes.desc: Wood-boring beetles recorded in large numbers on the island; they tunnel into woody plants and farm fungus in the galleries.

nodes.name: Cocos anole
nodes.desc: An endemic lizard of Cocos Island, one of the most recorded animals there, that hunts small insects.

nodes.name: Cocos flycatcher
nodes.desc: One of three endemic land birds; a small insect-catching bird of the island forest.

nodes.name: Red-footed booby
nodes.desc: Nests in large colonies on the island, often in trees. Plunge-dives for flying fish and squid far out to sea.

nodes.name: Great frigatebird
nodes.desc: Snatches flying fish from the sea surface and often follows tuna or dolphins that drive fish up. Also takes chicks of other seabirds.

nodes.name: Yellowfin tuna
nodes.desc: Fast open-water hunter of flying fish and other baitfish. Industrial fisheries are its main cause of death.

nodes.name: Bottlenose dolphin
nodes.desc: A frequently recorded marine mammal around the island, hunting fish and squid in open water.

nodes.name: Whale shark
nodes.desc: The biggest fish, a filter feeder on plankton, seen in the island waters.

nodes.name: Scalloped hammerhead
nodes.desc: Gathers around the island by day and hunts offshore at night, mainly bony fish and squid. Endangered, with near-pristine shark numbers here.

nodes.name: False killer whale
nodes.desc: A toothed whale that preys on large fish such as adult yellowfin tuna.
